note: Events: things that happen to Syracuse and its people, drawn from the game's state. Each has a trigger (when), the people it needs (roles), and defined choices with set effects. History events quote the saved source text they come from and list what the game invents (the trigger, the casting, every number). The engine is src/core/events.ts; the research card is docs/research/events-405-395.md.

events.name: The keeper's confession
events.text: Andron, who keeps the fortress and the treasure on the Island, comes to you at last. {Tempter} urged him to seize both while your back was turned. He confesses every detail, but he did not come to you at once.
events.why: Andron is trusted with the treasury, and {tempter} has no love for you

choices.label: Put Andron to death for his silence
choices.text: Andron dies for the days he kept quiet. {Tempter} is taken to prison. The court learns what a late confession costs.

effects.reason: you threw him in prison on Andron's word

choices.label: Thank Andron, and imprison {tempter}
choices.text: Andron weeps with relief. From now on he will tell you what he hears.

effects.reason: you threw him in prison on Andron's word

choices.label: Banish {tempter} to the Peloponnese, to spare the family

effects.reason: you banished him on Andron's word

choices.label: Say nothing, and have both watched

effects.why: he expected some answer from you

facts.text: Andron left in charge of fortress and treasury; Hermocrates urges him to seize them.
facts.quote: he left Andron in charge of the fortress and the treasury. Hermocrates advised Andron to seize both of these

facts.text: Executed for not reporting at once; the tempter imprisoned, then banished to please his wife.
facts.quote: because he had not revealed the proposal that had been made to him, immediately upon the tyrant's return

invented: who plays the tempter (Polyaenus names a Hermocrates, the sister's husband)
the choices other than execution and banishment

events.name: A flight by night
events.text: Polyxenus, your sister's husband, has become your enemy. At dawn word comes that, moved by fear, he slipped out of the city and is making for the coast.
events.why: Polyxenus holds a grudge against you, and fears what you will do

choices.label: Send riders after him

success.text: The riders bring Polyxenus back in chains.

effects.reason: you dragged him back in chains

failure.text: Polyxenus is gone, over the sea.

effects.reason: he fled from you into exile

choices.label: Write that he may come home safe

success.text: Polyxenus turns back, ashamed and grateful.

failure.text: Polyxenus does not believe a word of it.

effects.reason: he fled from you into exile

choices.label: Let him run

effects.reason: he fled from you into exile

facts.text: Polyxenus became an enemy and fled Sicily in fear. No date.
facts.quote: whose husband, Polyxenus, had become his enemy. When, therefore, Polyxenus was moved by fear to run away and go into exile from Sicily

invented: trigger (a grudge, and no warmth toward you)

events.name: Theste's answer
events.text: You send for your sister Theste and upbraid her: she knew of her husband's flight and did not tell you. She answers without fear. Had she known, she says, she would have sailed with him: "it would have been well for me to be called the wife of Polyxenus the exile, rather than the sister of Dionysius the tyrant."
events.why: her husband fled, and you think she knew

choices.label: Admire her boldness
choices.text: You let her go with honour. The city hears of it and admires her.

choices.label: Confine her to the women's rooms

effects.reason: you confined her for her husband's flight

choices.label: Send her after him

facts.text: Theste's answer.
facts.quote: it would have been well for me to be called the wife of Polyxenus the exile, rather than the sister of Dionysius the tyrant

facts.text: Dionysius admired her, and so did the Syracusans.
facts.quote: The tyrant is said to have admired Theste for this bold speech. And the Syracusans also admired the virtue of the woman

invented: the choices other than admiring her

events.name: No bride from Rhegium
events.text: You sent envoys to Rhegium asking for a bride from among its citizens, and promised them land and strength in return. After much debate their assembly has voted no.
events.why: you need children to secure your rule, and friends on the Strait before a war

choices.label: Send the same envoys to Locri
Swear that Rhegium will pay for this

effects.why: the cities on the Strait look to Carthage

choices.label: Take it quietly

effects.why: the rich families like a cautious ruler

facts.text: Rhegium votes against the marriage; Dionysius turns to Locri. About 398.
facts.quote: the Rhegians voted not to accept the marriage connection ... Now that Dionysius had failed of this design, he dispatched his ambassadors for the same purpose to the people of the Locrians

events.name: Two brides on one day
events.text: The Locrians agree to the match: Doris, daughter of Xenetus, their most esteemed citizen. In Syracuse the most notable maiden is Aristomache, daughter of Hipparinus. You could send your first quinquereme, fitted with silver and gold, for the one, and a chariot drawn by four white horses for the other.
events.why: Doris has come into the story, and Aristomache is unmarried

choices.label: Marry both on the same day, and feast the city
choices.text: You marry both on one day, and give public dinners for the soldiers and most of the citizens.

choices.label: Marry Doris of Locri alone

effects.why: you passed over his daughter for a foreigner

choices.label: Marry Aristomache alone
Not yet

facts.text: Doris of Locri and the quinquereme.
facts.quote: sued for the hand of Doris, the daughter of Xenetus, who at that time was their most esteemed citizen

facts.text: The chariot for Aristomache.
facts.quote: the most notable maiden among them, Aristomachê, for whom he dispatched a chariot drawn by four white horses

facts.text: Public dinners after both marriages.
facts.quote: After Dionysius had taken in marriage both maidens at the same time, he gave a series of public dinners for the soldiers and the larger part of the citizens

facts.text: Plutarch: both on one day.
facts.quote: It is said that he married both wives on one day

events.name: A son from Locri
events.text: Doris of Locri has borne you a son, your eldest. The city had hoped its own countrywoman would be honoured above the stranger.
events.why: Doris became a mother first

choices.label: Feast the birth before the whole city

effects.why: the Syracusans wished their countrywoman honoured above the stranger

choices.label: Give thanks quietly

facts.text: Doris bore the eldest son.
facts.quote: Doris had the good fortune to become a mother first, and by presenting Dionysius with his eldest son she atoned for her foreign birth

events.name: The charge against the Locrian mother
events.text: Aristomache has borne you no child. At court they whisper that the mother of your Locrian wife has been giving her drugs to prevent it.
events.why: Aristomache is still childless, and the court looks for someone to blame

choices.label: Accuse the Locrian mother and put her to death

effects.reason: you put her mother to death

effects.why: the court learns how far your suspicion reaches

choices.label: Dismiss the charge as court gossip
Send the mother home to Locri

facts.text: The charge and the execution. No date.
facts.quote: he accused the mother of his Locrian wife of giving Aristomache drugs to prevent conception, and put her to death

events.name: Counsel in the Island
events.text: Danger is close, and your friends gather in the Island to counsel you. It may be time to think not of how to win, but of how this ends.
events.why: a plot has been named, or the city is in revolt, or Carthage is at the walls

choices.label: Heloris: "Tyranny is a fair winding-sheet." Stand, and die a ruler if you must
Polyxenus: take your swiftest horse and ride for the Campanians

effects.text: You ride out of Syracuse on your swiftest horse. The tyranny is over; your life is not.

choices.label: Philistus: leave only when dragged out by the leg. Send for Campanian horsemen

effects.why: Campanian horsemen cut their way through to you

choices.label: Ask the city's leave to sail away with five ships, and wait
choices.text: The city believes the tyranny is ending. Men drift home to their fields.

effects.why: the plotters think they have already won

choices.label: Thank them, and decide nothing

facts.text: The council and the three counsels, about 404.
facts.quote: Heloris, one of his friends, or as some say, his adopted father, declared to him, "Tyranny is a fair winding-sheet"

facts.text: Polyxenus' advice.
facts.quote: advised him to use his swiftest horse and ride off into the domain of the Carthaginians to the Campanians

facts.text: Philistus' advice.
facts.quote: it was not fitting to dash from the tyranny on a galloping horse but to be cast out, dragged by the leg

facts.text: The five ships and the city relaxing.
facts.quote: having given the tyrant permission to sail away with five ships, took matters with rather less concern

invented: that it can come more than once

events.name: The Campanians' price
events.text: The Campanian horsemen you sent for have cut their way through to you. Now they want the price you promised.
events.why: you promised them any price they asked

choices.label: Pay them, and send them away
choices.text: They ride off. Word comes later that they took the town of Entella by treachery.

choices.label: Keep them on in the guard
Settle them on land

facts.text: Twelve hundred Campanian cavalry.
facts.quote: being in number twelve hundred cavalry

facts.text: Paid and sent away; they seize Entella.
facts.quote: To the Campanians he awarded the gifts that were due and then dispatched them from the city, having regard to their fickleness

invented: keeping them or giving them land

events.name: The Spartan envoy
events.text: Aristus, a distinguished Spartan, has landed. In public he promises the citizens their liberty. In private he tells you Sparta wants your rule made stronger, and that Nicoteles the Corinthian, a leader of the citizens, trusts him.
events.why: Sparta has won its war in Greece and wants friends in the west

choices.label: Let Aristus do his work
choices.text: Aristus kills Nicoteles, betraying the men who trusted him.

effects.why: Aristus betrayed those who trusted him

choices.label: Use him only to learn the citizens' plans
Send him home with gifts
Send him home with nothing

facts.text: Aristus pretends to free the city, kills Nicoteles. About 404.
facts.quote: promised to restore their liberty; then he slew Nicoteles the Corinthian, a leader of the Syracusans, made strong the tyrant by betraying those who put their faith in him

invented: the choices other than letting him

events.name: The empty houses
events.text: Harvest time. The citizens are out in the fields, and their houses in the city stand empty.
events.why: the citizens are Uneasy or worse, and the harvest takes them out of the city

choices.label: Search their houses and carry off their arms
choices.text: Your mercenaries go from house to house. When the citizens come home, their weapons are gone.

effects.why: you took their arms while they reaped

choices.label: Let them bring in the harvest

facts.text: Disarming the citizens at harvest, about 404.
facts.quote: sending the Syracusans out to harvest their crops, entered their homes and carried off the arms of them all

events.name: Sixty thousand hands
events.text: Your master-builders say the heights of Epipolae command the city. A wall there would mean Syracuse can never again be cut off from its countryside, as it was in the war with Athens.
events.why: Carthage stirs, and the heights are open

choices.label: Raise it in twenty days with the whole countryside, and work beside them
choices.text: You lay aside your dignity and haul stone with the workers. Some work into the night. The wall stands in twenty days.

choices.label: Pay for the wall, and leave the work to others
Not now

facts.text: Sixty thousand men on the wall, about 402/401.
facts.quote: he selected some sixty thousand capable men and parcelled out to them the space to be walled

facts.text: He worked beside them.
facts.quote: he laid aside the dignity of his office and reduced himself to the ranks

facts.text: Twenty days.
facts.quote: the wall was brought to completion in twenty days

events.name: The arms workshops
events.text: You could prepare for a great war: gather skilled workmen from your cities and, with high wages, from Italy, Greece and even Carthage's lands, and fill the porticoes and back rooms of the temples with forges.
events.why: a war with Carthage is coming, sooner or later

choices.label: Fill the city with workshops, and dine with the best workers
choices.text: The porticoes ring with hammers. Your engineers invent a new engine, the catapult.

choices.label: Order arms from abroad
Not yet

facts.text: Workmen gathered with high wages, about 399.
facts.quote: attracting them by high wages from Italy and Greece as well as Carthaginian territory

facts.text: The catapult invented; Dionysius among the workers.
facts.quote: the catapult was invented at this time in Syracuse

events.name: War, while Carthage is sick
events.text: Plague has struck Carthage and Libya. You could call the assembly and urge war now, before the enemy recovers.
events.why: Carthage is weak, and you are armed

choices.label: Declare war, and let the people plunder the Phoenicians in the city
choices.text: The assembly votes for war. The crowd strips the Phoenician merchants' houses and ships in the harbour.

choices.label: Declare war, but protect the merchants' goods
Keep the peace for now

facts.text: War urged while Carthage suffers plague, 398.
facts.quote: the Carthaginians were inactive because of the plague

facts.text: Phoenician property plundered.
facts.quote: the Syracusans, with the permission of Dionysius, seized as plunder the property of the Phoenicians

facts.text: The citizens hoped to win liberty with arms in hand.
facts.quote: once they had got weapons in their hand, they could strike for their liberty

events.name: Theodorus speaks for liberty
events.text: You call the assembly to praise the citizens and promise a quick end to the war. Before you can dismiss it, Theodorus, a man of action, held in high esteem among the cavalry, stands to speak for liberty: if you will lay down your office, let you leave with your possessions; if not, they have weapons in their hands and allies about them.
events.why: the war has put arms in the citizens' hands

choices.label: Look to the Spartan admiral to speak for you

mods.label: Spartan ships are in the harbour

success.text: The Spartan declares he came to fight Carthage, not to overthrow you. The mercenaries crowd around you; the citizens curse the Spartans and do nothing.

effects.reason: the Spartans shouted down his call for liberty

failure.text: No one speaks for you. The assembly breaks up in uproar, and Theodorus' name is on every tongue.

effects.why: the assembly would not hear you, and he saw it

choices.label: Have the guard drag Theodorus from the platform

effects.reason: you had him dragged from the assembly

choices.label: Promise to lay down your power when the war is won
Dissolve the assembly, then win the crowd back with gifts and banquets

effects.reason: you shut the assembly on his speech

choices.label: Dissolve the assembly

effects.reason: you shut the assembly on his speech

facts.text: Theodorus rises, about 396.
facts.quote: Theodorus, a Syracusan, who was held in high esteem among the cavalry and was considered a man of action, made bold to speak

facts.text: His demand.
facts.quote: if he is willing to lay down his office of his own accord, let us allow him to leave the city with his possessions

facts.text: Pharacidas vetoes.
facts.quote: not to overthrow the rule of Dionysius

facts.text: Gifts and banquets after.
facts.quote: later he won the favour of the multitude by kindly words, honouring some of them with gifts and inviting some to general banquets

invented: the roll for the Spartan's answer

events.name: An embassy for ships
events.text: Carthage is coming. You could send your brother-in-law Polyxenus to the Greeks of Italy, to Sparta and to Corinth, begging for ships, with ample money to hire soldiers.
events.why: the Carthage clock is high, and Polyxenus is on good terms with you

choices.label: Send Polyxenus with ample funds
Rely on your own ships

facts.text: Polyxenus sent as ambassador, about 396.
facts.quote: sent his brother-in-law Polyxenus as ambassador both to the Greeks in Italy and to the Lacedaemonians, as well as the Corinthians

events.name: Thirty ships from the allies
events.text: Polyxenus is back from the Peloponnese and Italy, bringing thirty warships from your allies, with the Spartan Pharacidas as admiral.
events.why: the embassy you sent

facts.text: Thirty warships under Pharacidas.
facts.quote: bringing thirty warships from his allies, with Pharacidas the Lacedaemonian as admiral

events.name: The mercenaries want their pay
events.text: The mercenaries are hostile, and you fear they may depose you. They gather under arms and demand their pay, with some sharpness.
events.why: the guard is unpaid and Uneasy or worse

choices.label: Arrest Aristotle, send him to Sparta for trial, and give the men land at Leontini instead of pay

effects.why: sent to Sparta to face trial

effects.reason: you arrested him and sent him to Sparta

effects.why: many go off to farm at Leontini

choices.label: Go out to them in mean clothes, with dust on your head, and give yourself up to them

success.text: Seeing you so humbled, they cannot bring themselves to touch you.

failure.text: They jeer. Someone shoves you, and no one stops him.

effects.why: the guard has seen you humbled

choices.label: Promise them pay soon

facts.text: Aristotle arrested; Leontini given instead of pay, about 396.
facts.quote: offered to the mercenaries, who numbered about ten thousand, in lieu of their pay the city and territory of the Leontines

facts.text: Dust on his head.
facts.quote: He came out to them in mean clothes, with dust on his head

events.name: Carthage's secret offer
events.text: Beaten back, the Carthaginian general sends to you in secret, behind the citizens' backs: let his own Carthaginians sail home by night, and three hundred talents are yours.
events.why: Carthage's army was thrown back from the walls

choices.label: Take the silver, and let them slip away
choices.text: The silver comes to the Island by night. Carthage lives to come again, and the citizens stay afraid of it.

effects.why: Carthage keeps an army to come back with
fear of Carthage keeps the city close to you

choices.label: Refuse, and destroy them on the shore

facts.text: Three hundred talents for a secret retreat, 396.
facts.quote: promised to give him the three hundred talents which they had there in their camp

facts.text: His reason, as Diodorus gives it.
facts.quote: should never find a time of ease to assert their freedom

events.name: The captain's dream
events.text: {Dreamer}, whom you raised to high command, dreamed of killing you and told the dream over wine. The story is all through the barracks.
events.why: you are suspicious, and in the barracks dreams get told

choices.label: Put {dreamer} to death: what a man dreams by night, he plans by day

effects.why: no one dares even dream against you

choices.label: Laugh it off, and toast {dreamer} at dinner
Have {dreamer} watched

facts.text: Marsyas killed for a dream. No date.
facts.quote: he slew Marsyas, one of those whom he had advanced to positions of high command, for having dreamed that he killed him

invented: who dreams (Plutarch names Marsyas, who is not in the cast; a member of the guard takes his place)

events.name: The borrowed spear
events.text: Describing a place to you, Leptines drew its plan on the ground with a spear he took from one of your bodyguards. No one is meant to bear arms in your presence.
events.why: you trust no one near you with a weapon, not even your brother

choices.label: Put to death the guard who handed over the spear

effects.why: no guard will let a weapon near you again

choices.label: Rebuke Leptines before the court

effects.reason: you shamed him before the court

choices.label: Let it pass

facts.text: Leptines and the spear. No date.
facts.quote: drew the plan of it on the ground with a spear which he took from one of his body-guards, he was extremely angry with him, and had the man who gave him the spear put to death

events.name: A marriage made without you
events.text: Leptines has given one of his two daughters to Philistus in marriage, without so much as telling you.
events.why: Leptines and Philistus are close, and neither asked you

choices.label: Banish Philistus from Sicily, and put Leptines' wife in fetters

effects.reason: you banished him for his marriage
you put his wife in fetters

choices.label: Bless the match
Accept it, but make plain the choice was yours to make

facts.text: The marriage and the banishment. Plutarch gives no date; it may fall after 395.
facts.quote: gave one of them to Philistus without so much as telling Dionysius, the tyrant was wroth, put the wife of Leptines into fetters and prison, and banished Philistus from Sicily

invented: that it can happen in 405 to 395 at all

events.name: The man with the secret
events.text: A foreigner in the city claims an infallible secret for revealing conspiracies, and will tell it to you alone. Alone with you, he says: claim, as I do, that you have such a secret, and no one will dare plot against you.
events.why: a clever stranger has heard how much you fear plots

choices.label: Reward him well, and tell your guards what he "revealed"

effects.why: everyone believes you can see plots coming

choices.label: Have him thrown out

facts.text: The foreigner's advice. No date.
facts.quote: Only claim, as I have done, that you possess the secret which I am pretending to reveal; and no-one will venture into any conspiracy against you

events.name: What the musicians hear
events.text: Your agents say the flute-girls and courtesans of the city hear everything their lovers say about you.
events.why: you want to know who your enemies are

choices.label: Have them questioned under torture

effects.why: the city hears what was done to them

choices.label: Pay them for what they hear

failure.text: They tell you only what you want to hear.

choices.label: Leave them be

facts.text: Musicians and courtesans questioned. No date.
facts.quote: they were made to confess under torture, what were the opinions which they had heard their lovers express about the tyranny

events.name: A report of your death
events.text: Your enemies are stirring. You could put out word that you are at the point of death, and watch who rejoices.
events.why: there are whispers of a plot

choices.label: Feign a mortal illness, and mark who rejoices

success.text: You appear in public with your guards, and the men who rejoiced go pale.

effects.why: they see how you test them

failure.text: The rumour runs ahead of you. The city thinks you weak.

effects.why: the plotters think you are failing

choices.label: Do not tempt the gods

facts.text: The feigned illness. No date.
facts.quote: Dionysius pretended to be ill, and ordered a report to be spread about, that he was at the point of death

events.name: Demeter's ornaments
events.text: The treasury is empty. You could tell the assembly that Demeter has appeared to you and asked for the women's ornaments to be brought to her temple, as your own household has already done.
events.why: you are short of silver

choices.label: Proclaim the goddess's wish, then borrow her gold
Leave the gods out of it

facts.text: The ornaments of Demeter. No date.
facts.quote: declared that Demeter had appeared to him, and bade him convey all the women’s ornaments into her temple

events.name: Coins of tin
events.text: You hold the mint and have no silver. You could strike coins of tin, and have the assembly vote that whatever a man receives counts as silver.
events.why: you are short of silver, and you hold the mint

choices.label: Strike the tin, and have the vote passed

effects.why: their wealth is paid back in tin

choices.label: Keep the coin honest

facts.text: Tin coinage. No date.
facts.quote: he minted a coinage of tin

events.name: The offerings of Asclepius
events.text: The people refuse a new tax: they have paid too often already. Meanwhile the temple of Asclepius is full of offerings of silver and gold.
events.why: the treasury is low, and the people will not pay

choices.label: Sell the god's offerings in the market, then order the buyers to give them back
Let the temple be

facts.text: The temple offerings sold and reclaimed. No date.
facts.quote: whoever had sacrilegiously bought any of the offerings from the temple of Asclepius, should on pain of death immediately return them to the temple

events.name: Sharing out the land
events.text: The land of Syracuse is yours to share out. Your friends and officers expect the best of it. The freed slaves could be enrolled as citizens.
events.why: after the troubles, the land is yours to give

choices.label: Give the best land to friends and officers
Free slaves, and enrol them as New Citizens
Divide it equally among citizens and resident foreigners
Keep the land for now

facts.text: Land to friends and officers, equal portions to the rest, freedmen as New Citizens. About 404.
facts.quote: including under the name of citizens the manumitted slaves whom he designated as New Citizens

invented: making the three into separate choices (Diodorus has him do all of them)

events.name: Words in the ranks
events.text: In camp the citizen soldiers, arms in hand, gather in groups and reproach each other for not joining the cavalry against you. Doricus, their commander, warned one outspoken man; the man answered back, and Doricus stepped up to strike him.
events.why: the citizens are armed for the campaign, and Uneasy or worse

choices.label: Back Doricus: discipline first

success.text: The man is flogged and the ranks fall silent.

failure.text: The soldiers kill Doricus and cry to the citizens to strike for their freedom.

choices.label: Order Doricus to stand down
Break off the campaign and hurry home

facts.text: Doricus killed at Herbessus, about 404.
facts.quote: The soldiers, in anger at this, slew the commander, whose name was Doricus

facts.text: Dionysius broke off the siege.
facts.quote: broke off the siege and hastened to Syracuse

invented: the roll that decides whether Doricus dies

events.name: Terms for Aetna
events.text: You could bury the dead of both sides with honour, and send envoys to the exiles at Aetna pledging that you bear them no enmity if they come home.
events.why: thousands of exiles still hold Aetna

choices.label: Offer terms to all the exiles

mods.label: the rich families are Content or better

success.text: Men who left wives and children in the city come home. The rest stay at Aetna.

failure.text: The exiles answer that you deserve the same favour as the dead, and pray the gods grant it soon.

effects.reason: you offered terms no exile could trust

choices.label: Let them rot at Aetna

facts.text: Terms offered, about 404.
facts.quote: asking the exiles to accept terms and return to their native land, and giving his pledged word that he would not bear enmity against them

facts.text: Some came back; the rest prayed he would die.
facts.quote: they prayed to the gods that they might, the sooner the better, see him obtain it

events.name: Leptines wants battle
events.text: Leptines, your admiral, wants to take the thirty best ships far ahead of the rest and fall on the Carthaginian fleet.
events.why: Carthage's fleet is near, and Leptines commands yours

choices.label: Let him attack

success.text: Leptines sinks a good part of the enemy's van and comes home in glory.

failure.text: Leptines fights bravely but without prudence, is driven off, and flees to the open sea. Many ships are lost.

choices.label: Order him to keep the line

facts.text: Leptines at Catana, 397/396.
facts.quote: Leptines advanced with his thirty best vessels far ahead of the rest and joined battle, in no cowardly fashion, but without prudence

events.name: The old soldiers' pay
events.text: The soldiers' pay weighs on the treasury. You could stop paying the old veterans, but the young men say it would be cruel to starve those who spent their youth in your service.
events.why: the guard costs more than the treasury takes in

choices.label: Post the old men to the forts at equal pay, then stop their pay once they are scattered

effects.why: the trick on the veterans gets out

choices.label: Keep paying them

facts.text: The veterans' pay. No date.
facts.quote: Dionysius wished to deprive the old soldiers of their pay

events.name: Wine at your table
events.text: At your dinner, deep in the wine, {mocker} mocks {target} before the whole table. Everyone looks at you.
events.why: wine loosens tongues

choices.label: Laugh along with {mocker}

effects.reason: you laughed at him at your own table

choices.label: Rebuke {mocker}
Send them both home
Change the subject

events.name: A debt called in
events.text: {Lender} reminds you, politely and then less politely, that you owe him.
events.why: you borrowed from {lender}

choices.label: Repay him with interest
Repay him with a voice at court instead
Tell him the debt can wait

effects.reason: you would not repay what you owed

events.name: A house in ruin
events.text: {Debtor}'s house is ruined by debt. Creditors circle the estates.
events.why: bad years, bad loans

choices.label: Lend {debtor} enough to stand
Buy the estates cheap

effects.reason: you bought his estates for nothing

choices.label: Let the creditors have them

events.name: A match between houses

events.name: Your promise comes due
events.text: The citizens remember your promise to lay down your power once the war was won. They are waiting.
events.why: you promised the assembly

choices.label: Keep your word, and step down

effects.text: You lay down your power and live on in Syracuse as a private man. The city remembers that a tyrant once kept his word.

Say the danger is not yet past

events.name: A sword on a horse-hair
events.text: Over dinner {flatterer} praises your wealth and your power, and swears there was never a man more fortunate than you. You could offer to let {flatterer} taste that fortune for a day.
events.why: {flatterer} flatters you, and wants what you have

choices.label: Seat {flatterer} on your golden couch, with a sword hung over the couch by a single horse-hair
choices.text: The boys serve, the tables are piled high, and {flatterer} feels fortunate until looking up. After that the food goes untouched, the garlands slip, and {flatterer} begs to be let go, no longer wanting to be fortunate. The court tells the story for years.

effects.why: you frightened him before the court
the court sees that you know what hangs over you

choices.label: Accept the praise, and reward {flatterer}
Smile, and say nothing

events.source: Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5.57 to 5.61 (Latin saved; the story is 5.61)

facts.text: Damocles, a flatterer, praises the tyrant's fortune.
facts.quote: one of his flatterers, Damocles, mentioned in conversation the wealth of Dionysius

facts.text: The offer.
facts.quote: do you wish to taste it yourself and make trial of my fortune?

facts.text: The sword.
facts.quote: a shining sword, fastened from the ceiling by a horse-hair

facts.text: He asks to leave.
facts.quote: he begged the tyrant that he should be allowed to depart because he no longer wanted to be fortunate.

facts.text: Cicero's tyrant ruled 38 years, from the age of 25: Dionysius I, the game's ruler.
facts.quote: Duodequadraginta annos tyrannus Syracusanorum fuit Dionysius, cum quinque et viginti natus annos dominatum occupavisset

facts.text: His two wives are Aristomache of Syracuse and Doris of Locri, the wives of Dionysius I.
facts.quote: Aristomachen civem suam, Doridem autem Locrensem

facts.text: The Damocles story is told of this same tyrant.
facts.quote: Quamquam hic quidem tyrannus ipse iudicavit

facts.text: A modern page disagrees: Livius.org's introduction gives the story to Dionysius II, against Cicero's own text.
facts.quote: the tyrant Dionysius II of Syracuse

invented: who plays Damocles (Damocles is not in the cast; a friendly courtier takes his place)
the choices other than the sword
when it happens: Cicero gives no year, so the event may come any season from Spring 404
events.note: Settled 2026-11-22: Cicero 5.57 and 5.59 show the tyrant is Dionysius I. Only the timing is invention.

events.name: No blade at your throat
events.text: Your beard has grown long, and the barber waits in the courtyard with his razor. There is a plot somewhere in the city, and a barber's hand rests on a man's throat.
events.why: a plot is afoot, and every blade near you is a question

choices.label: Sit for the barber, as other men do
choices.text: The barber shaves you and goes. The city hears that you still sit in a barber's chair.

effects.why: he sits for the barber like any citizen
a stranger's blade at your throat every month

choices.label: Have the women of your house learn the barber's trade
choices.text: The women of your house learn a slave's trade and shave you themselves. The court whispers about it.

effects.why: the women of his house made to do a slave's work
no stranger's blade comes near him

choices.label: Let no blade near you: have your beard singed off with hot walnut shells
choices.text: Glowing walnut shells are brought, and your beard and hair are singed away. No iron touches you.

effects.why: no blade comes near his throat
the city hears he fears even a razor

facts.text: He would not trust his neck to a barber, and taught his daughters to shave him.
facts.quote: Quin etiam ne tonsori collum committeret, tondere filias suas docuit.

facts.text: A mean, slavish craft, Cicero says.
facts.quote: Ita sordido ancillarique artificio regiae virgines ut tonstriculae tondebant barbam et capillum patris.

facts.text: When they were grown, he took the blades from them too, and had his beard singed with hot walnut shells.
facts.quote: ut candentibus iuglandium putaminibus barbam sibi et capillum adurerent.

invented: the women of the house instead of his daughters: Dionysius' daughters were born after his marriages of 398 and could not be grown in this decade, so the game gives the trade to his household
the walnut shells without the daughters

events.name: A bed behind a trench
events.text: You are married now, and at night you go to {wife}'s rooms through dark corridors. Any door could hide a knife, and any bed could be a trap.
events.why: you sleep where anyone can reach you

choices.label: Have her rooms searched before each visit, and sleep behind a broad trench crossed by a little wooden bridge you draw up yourself
choices.text: Workmen dig a trench round your bed. Each night you search, cross the little bridge, close the door and pull the bridge up after you.

effects.why: the household is searched every night

choices.label: Post guards at your door, and leave {wife} in peace

effects.why: the guard keeps the tyrant's bedroom

choices.label: Trust {wife}, and sleep as other men do

facts.text: His two wives, Aristomache of Syracuse and Doris of Locri.
facts.quote: Cumque duas uxores haberet, Aristomachen civem suam, Doridem autem Locrensem,

facts.text: He came to them at night only after searching everything.
facts.quote: sic noctu ad eas ventitabat, ut omnia specularetur et perscrutaretur ante.

facts.text: A broad trench round his bed, crossed by a little wooden bridge.
facts.quote: Et cum fossam latam cubiculari lecto circumdedisset eiusque fossae transitum ponticulo ligneo coniunxisset,

facts.text: He drew the bridge up himself once the door was shut.

events.name: A voice from a tower

choices.label: Speak from a high tower
choices.text: Your voice comes down from the tower. The people hear the words and do not see the man.

effects.why: he speaks to them from a tower

choices.label: Stand on the common platform, among them
choices.text: You stand where every speaker stands. The crowd presses close, and you come down unharmed.

effects.why: he let the crowd come close

choices.label: Send a herald to read your words
choices.text: A herald reads your words. The assembly listens politely and goes home.

facts.text: He did not dare stand on the common platforms, and used to address the people from a high tower.
facts.quote: Idemque cum in communibus suggestis consistere non auderet, contionari ex turri alta solebat.

events.name: A joke at the ball game
events.text: You strip off your tunic to play ball, and hand your sword to {favourite}, a young man you are fond of. {joker}, a friend of the house, jokes: "Him, at least, you trust with your life." {favourite} laughs.

choices.text: Both are dead before evening. Nobody at court jokes about your sword again.

effects.why: two men killed over a joke

choices.label: Take your sword back, and play no more today
choices.text: You take back the sword without a word. The game breaks up, and {favourite} goes home ashamed.

choices.label: Laugh with them, and play on

facts.quote: adulescentulo, quem amabat, tradidisse gladium dicitur.

facts.text: He had both killed: one for showing the way to kill him, the other for approving it with a laugh.
